messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kelepi traces the grain of the wood on his drafting table, a motion that once brought him comfort but now feels hollow. At sixty-seven, he had envisioned a gentle winding down of his interior design practice, a celebrated career culminating in passion projects and time with his grandchildren. Instead, his world has shrunk to the dimensions of this one room. The change began three years ago, on what was supposed to be a routine sourcing trip to North Africa. The details of his abduction remain a chaotic blur, a series of disjointed sensory snapshots. What he remembers with sickening clarity is the suffocating darkness of the storeroom where he was held for nineteen days. The coarse texture of the burlap sack over his head, the cold concrete floor, and above all, the sounds. The guttural, angry shouts in Arabic from the hallway were a constant torment, a language he didn't understand but whose menacing tone needed no translation.

In the first year after his release, Kelepi tried to reclaim his life. He threw himself back into his work, but the familiar spaces of his profession had become hostile territory. While measuring a walk-in closet for a client, the closing of the door behind him plunged the small space into shadow, and suddenly he was back on the concrete floor, the smell of dust and fear filling his lungs. He fled the appointment, leaving his equipment behind. This became a pattern. Elevators, windowless bathrooms, even client meetings in small conference rooms became impossible. He began turning down lucrative jobs, making excuses that grew increasingly flimsy. His business, once his pride, is now nearly defunct.

His body remains on high alert, a sentinel that never stands down. A car backfiring on the street sends him diving for cover before his mind can even label the sound; his heart hammers against his ribs, a frantic drumbeat of pure terror, long after he recognizes the source. He feels profoundly unsafe unless his back is to a wall, his eyes scanning every entrance. When his daughter invites him for dinner, he spends the hour before she arrives rehearsing the conversation, planning his answers to simple questions like "How are you?" because the thought of being caught off guard, of feeling emotionally exposed, is intolerable. He has come to believe that any strong feeling is a sign of weakness, a vulnerability that could lead to disaster. The fear and shame are a constant, bitter taste in his mouth.

The memories of those nineteen days are a cruel paradox. Sometimes, when a news report mentions the Middle East, a memory will flash into his mind, unbidden and complete with the auditory echo of his captors' voices. He can hear the shouting as if it were happening right now, in his sunlit studio. Yet, when he tries to intentionally explain what happened to his concerned daughter, the narrative collapses. He loses the thread, the sequence of events becomes muddled, and he trails off, frustrated by his inability to articulate his own story. At other times, he can recount the facts of his captivity with a chilling detachment, feeling absolutely nothing, as if he is describing a character in a film he once saw. It is this fragmentation that frightens him most—the sense that the experience is both intensely present and completely inaccessible, a part of him that he can neither integrate nor escape. It was after one such attempt to explain, seeing the helpless worry in his daughter's eyes as he fell into confused silence, that Kelepi finally agreed to seek help. He holds little hope of feeling like his old self again, but he is desperate for an end to the siege within his own mind.
